title: Exclusive-US has used 'virtually all' of its long-range precision missiles during Iran war, sources say
description: , Mike Stone and Jonathan Landay NEW YORK/WASHINGTON, Aug 4 (Reuters) - The U.S.
fullText:
NEW YORK/WASHINGTON, Aug 4 (Reuters) - The U.S. Army has used up much of its stockpile of highly accurate long-range missiles during its five-month war with Iran, according to three people familiar with the data, raising concerns about the military's readiness for future conflicts.

The missiles are principally the Army's surface-to-surface weapons, known as Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM). The U.S. has used "virtually ‌all" of these weapons, according to two of the sources.

The degree to which the military is running out of ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles has not been previously reported.

The long-range munitions – which cost more than $1 million each – are ‌an important part of the military's arsenal, allowing accurate strikes from a safe distance. U.S.-supplied ATACMS have played a key role in the war in Ukraine, allowing Ukrainian forces to attack targets inside Russia. The PrSM is a newer, more advanced generation that will replace the ATACMS, which have a shorter range.

The dramatic ​rundown in precision, long-range missiles means U.S. President Donald Trump may have to rely more on riskier, piloted bombing missions if he relaunches large-scale attacks on Iran.

The sources declined to say how many of each munition the U.S. had left.

Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February, predicting that the conflict would last a short time.

But as the war drags on, the three people familiar with the matter expressed worry that the falling missile supplies could limit the U.S. ability to deter adversaries, including Russia and China.

A fourth person familiar with the matter said that while Central Command — which oversees U.S. forces in the Middle East — has nearly used up the land-based missiles it had before the war began, it has been able to reload from U.S. military supplies elsewhere in the world.

The sources interviewed ‌for this story spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Asked for comment on the stockpile ⁠data, the White House issued a statement from Trump, saying the U.S. had "far more munitions than anyone in the world" and "far more than we need."

"Our defense companies are, at this moment, making more munitions than they have ever made before, in addition to expanding their plants and equipment at record levels," Trump said.

Analysts agree that certain munitions, including artillery shells and several types of missiles, are being ⁠produced at record levels but caution that supplies might fall short of what is needed for a prolonged war.

Lockheed Martin, which makes the ATACMS and PrSMs, along with the anti-ballistic missile THAAD system, did not immediately respond to questions about Trump's statements or about supply levels. Raytheon, which makes Tomahawk missiles and Patriot interceptors, two important U.S. weapons, also did not immediately respond.

Responding to a request for comment, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said: "America's military is the most powerful in the world and has everything it needs to execute at the time and place of the President's ​choosing. ​We have executed multiple successful operations across combatant commands while ensuring the U.S. military possesses a deep arsenal of capabilities to protect our people and ​our interests."

The supply figures have circulated inside the federal government over the last week during tense ‌conversations inside the Trump administration about how much longer the U.S. can continue striking Iran without drawing down the stockpile to levels that would limit the military's ability to respond to crises elsewhere.

One of the sources said the drawdown of the ATACMS and PrSM stockpiles reflected a decision by the Trump administration to avoid riskier ways of attacking Iranian targets, such as by using piloted aircraft to drop bombs.

Because these weapons allow the military to attack targets from a distance, analysts say they would be valuable in a war against an adversary with strong air defenses, such as China. They have been used to strike targets inside Iran, according to a March report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

According to the report, PrSM stockpiles were low to start with, since it is a relatively new munition, but the U.S. military has ordered a large number of them for 2027. The Army has said that ATACMS are being phased out and that production is shifting to the newer PrSM missiles.

Military ‌leaders have for weeks warned the president that stockpiles of defensive weapons — including Patriot interceptors, which are effective against ballistic missiles — were dwindling, said ​two of the sources. Last week, several media outlets reported Trump had decided not to launch another massive offensive inside Iran in part because his ​military advisers had warned about the U.S. stockpile.

A U.S. official disputed those accounts, saying Trump chose not to move forward ​with another attack because of pressure from Gulf states.

The Middle East conflict has sparked intense debate about Trump's authority to prosecute hostilities against Iran without congressional authorization. No request for a declaration of war ‌or an authorization to use military force has been submitted to Congress.

DEFENSIVE WEAPON STOCKS ARE ALSO ​DIMINISHED

Last week, CSIS published a report estimating that between February and ​July about 65% of Patriot interceptors had been expended and that the number of THAAD ballistic missile interceptors in U.S. stockpiles was at least 38% lower than at the start of the war. Patriots and THAADs are systems that detect and destroy incoming missiles and are among the most effective in the country's arsenal.

While Reuters has not seen the supply figures, those numbers match internal U.S. data, two of the sources said.

The U.S. also burned through a little ​less than half of its global supply of Tomahawk cruise missiles, which are generally launched from ‌ships, since the start of the war, one of the sources said.

The Tomahawk is a Navy weapon, launched from destroyers, cruisers and submarines, and has long served as the sea ​service's principal means of striking heavily defended targets without risking pilots.

Raytheon, a unit of RTX, has reached a tentative multi-year agreement with the Pentagon aimed at boosting Tomahawk production, alongside increases in other munitions, as ​Washington races to rebuild stockpiles.

title: Attorney who defended DC sniper says Kohberger faces 'monumental uphill battle' undoing guilty plea
description: A criminal defense attorney explains why Bryan Kohberger's effort to undo his University of Idaho murders guilty plea faces two significant legal hurdles.
fullText:
Bryan Kohberger faces a "monumental uphill battle" in his effort to withdraw his guilty plea in the murders of four University of Idaho students, according to an attorney who represented D.C. sniper Lee Boyd Malvo and once helped another client successfully withdraw a guilty plea before winning an acquittal.

Mark Petrovich, who represented Malvo in post-conviction proceedings in Virginia and has decades of criminal defense experience, told Fox News Digital that defendants rarely succeed in withdrawing guilty pleas after sentencing, even in cases involving claims that they were unaware of potentially exculpatory evidence before entering the plea.

He cautioned against drawing direct comparisons between Malvo's post-conviction litigation and Kohberger's effort to withdraw his guilty plea. Malvo's appeals stemmed from changes in constitutional law governing juvenile sentencing, while Kohberger is attempting to undo a plea agreement he entered as an adult after avoiding the death penalty.

Kaylee Goncalves' Mother Says Family Ready For Trial After Bryan Kohberger Seeks To Withdraw Guilty Plea

"It's a monumental uphill battle," Petrovich said. "First of all, getting the judge to allow you to withdraw the plea, and then second of all to winning any new proceeding, because there's a lot against you."

Kohberger pleaded guilty in July 2025 to the stabbing deaths of University of Idaho students Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle, Madison Mogen and Kaylee Goncalves in Moscow, Idaho, in November 2022. He was sentenced to four consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole after accepting a plea agreement that spared him from the death penalty.

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

In recent court filings, Kohberger claimed he was pressured into accepting the plea agreement, did not fully understand potentially exculpatory evidence before pleading guilty and was misled about the conditions he would face while incarcerated.

Idaho Murders: New Book On Kohberger Reveals Previously Unseen Evidence, Claims Sheath Could Be Inadmissible

He contends those factors undermined the voluntariness of his decision to plead guilty.

Petrovich said he once represented a client who sought to withdraw a guilty plea before sentencing. A judge granted the request, the case proceeded to trial and the client was acquitted, but he said Kohberger's circumstances are fundamentally different because he has already been sentenced.

"You can't wait until after you're sentenced and see what the consequences of the plea are and then change your plea," Petrovich said. "It's going to be a very, very difficult burden to overcome."

Alex Murdaugh Murder Saga Lands Right Back Where It Started Before Next Lowcountry Courtroom Battle

Petrovich said Kohberger would face two significant hurdles even if a judge allowed him to withdraw his plea.

One would be convincing jurors after previously admitting guilt under oath.

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

Even if a judge allowed Kohberger to withdraw his plea, Petrovich said jurors would almost certainly learn he had already admitted guilt, creating another significant obstacle at trial.

"One thing that's important is that you still can't hide from the jury the fact that you said under oath that you're guilty," Petrovich said. "Even if you withdraw, then you have to explain that ... if you're going to get anywhere with any kind of jury finding."

Petrovich also questioned whether Kohberger's attorneys would have advised him to accept a plea agreement without first reviewing the evidence disclosed during discovery.

He noted that defense attorneys handling capital cases typically spend years reviewing discovery before recommending whether a client should plead guilty.

"The attorneys on the case ... were intimately familiar with the evidence and the information that was provided to them by law enforcement and prosecution," Petrovich said. "I'm sure they knew all about everything. If they encouraged him or if there was a discussion and a plea was decided on, I'm sure it was for good reason."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Kohberger's case is not the first involving a notorious killer who later sought to undo a guilty plea.

James Earl Ray pleaded guilty in 1969 to assassinating the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. to avoid a potential death sentence. Three days after entering his guilty plea, Ray sought to withdraw it, arguing he had been pressured into confessing. He spent the rest of his life trying to undo the plea but died in prison in 1998 without ever receiving the jury trial he sought.

Serial killer Clifton Bloomfield unsuccessfully sought to withdraw guilty pleas after admitting to five murders in New Mexico to avoid capital punishment. Washington serial killer Robert Lee Yates Jr. also challenged his plea agreement after admitting to murdering 13 women, but courts ultimately rejected both efforts.

Kohberger's plea agreement spared him from facing a capital trial and ended years of pretrial litigation in one of the country's most closely watched murder prosecutions.

Petrovich said that history, combined with the years of discovery and plea negotiations leading up to Kohberger's agreement, makes the effort to withdraw it especially difficult.

title: 60,000 residents evacuated as Washington wildfires rage on
description: Firefighters in the Spokane area continue to battle the blaze.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — Wildfires in eastern Washington state have forced tens of thousands from their homes and scorched more than 250,000 acres.

Firefighters in the Spokane area continue to battle the blaze, which has destroyed at least 600 structures so far. Damage assessment crews are working to collect more specific information on the destruction caused by the fires.

Cooler temperatures and higher humidity on Sunday allowed firefighters to make significant gains on the Old Trails and Fairview fires, with the Autumn Lane fire remaining active. Suppression eforts are continuing, authorities said Monday.

A temporary flight restriction has been put in place over the fires, with 26 reported drone incursions in the fire. Authorities warned that such incursions can impact firefighting efforts, with the potential to shut down aerial fire suppression for safety reasons.

The fires in and around Spokane, the state's second-largest city, burned about 8.2 square miles over the weekend and were among dozens of wildfires across the Western U.S. that stretched the ability of federal, state and local agencies to fight them.

A total of about 390 square miles has burned across the state, and some of the fires, including those in the Spokane area, have not been contained.

At this time, there have been no reports of injuries or people unaccounted for.

Local fire officials are telling residents to help out their neighbors as people are forced to leave their homes behind while the fires rage on.

"Reach out to someone you know who has been affected. Offer a meal, a place to stay, help with errands, or simply let them know they are not alone. Small acts of kindness can make a bigger difference than you realize," read a post from the Spokane County Fire District 9.

Washington Rep. Michael Baumgartner wrote on X that he has spoken with DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Washington state Gov. Bob Ferguson to get federal assistance for the wildfire.

title: Eala becomes first Filipino to win WTA singles title
description: Alexandra Eala becomes the first Filipino to win a WTA singles title as she beats top seed Jessica Pegula in a delayed Washington Open final.
fullText:
Alexandra Eala became the first Filipino to win a WTA singles title as she beat top seed Jessica Pegula in a delayed Washington Open final.

The WTA showpiece was postponed from Sunday to Monday because of bad weather in the US capital.

Rain and lightning meant the start was pushed back on Sunday, before world number three Pegula took the first set 6-4.

Eala, 21, was leading 2-1 in the second set when further bad weather meant play was halted and then cancelled for the rest of the day.

And after play resumed on Monday, Pegula won just three more games as Eala wrapped up a 4-6 6-4 6-0 victory.

Pegula, 32, previously won the event in 2019 and 2021, but Eala secured the second set before racing through the decider behind a dominant left-handed serve and some fearless baseline hitting.

"I feel so much love," she said. "I knew whatever happened, this match would have already been a win for me.

"My first chance at a title knowing it won't be the last and already [I've] achieved this milestone for my career."

Eala will jump from 28th in the world rankings to a career-high 20 and before the final Pegula described her as "the future of the tour".

On Monday, the American added: "To see how far you've come over the last couple of years since we first played, to see the amazing fans that follow you every place you go, it's not fun to play against, but I think it's amazing."

The victory extended Eala's winning streak against top-10 opponents to five matches following victories over Elena Rybakina, Elina Svitolina (twice), and Iga Swiatek.

title: Analysis-How Iran is widening its pressure campaign to force US concessions

fullText:
BEIRUT, Aug 3 (Reuters) - Iran is betting it can outlast Washington by turning the Middle East's trade routes, shipping lanes and energy infrastructure into pressure points that steadily raise the cost of confrontation, according to Gulf officials and analysts.

Rather than seeking a decisive military victory, Tehran is pursuing a strategy of calibrated escalation aimed at widening the conflict without triggering full-scale war.

The ‌goal, they say, is to convince the United States and its allies that containing the crisis is more costly than accommodating Iran's demands over the Strait of Hormuz.

The message from Tehran is that unless ‌Washington accepts a new status quo that gives Iran a greater role in Hormuz, the conflict could spread beyond the Gulf.

"Iran, from the beginning, has tried to out-escalate ​the United States by stretching out its escalation options so that it always has something new to bring every week -- a new geography, a new type of weapon, a new type of target," Michael Knights of the Washington Institute told Reuters.

"The bigger advantage they have is not that they can hurt America or Israel," Knights added. "Their big advantage is that they can hurt the regional states and the global economy."

EXPANDING THREATS BEYOND HORMUZ

Having demonstrated its ability to disrupt traffic through Hormuz, through which about a fifth of global oil consumption flowed before the war, Tehran has signalled that no maritime chokepoint is off limits.

Threats to the Red Sea and Saudi energy infrastructure suggest a broader effort to raise the cost of protecting global ‌commerce while testing Washington's tolerance for disruption.

Iran's approach reflects what one Gulf source ⁠described as a belief among Revolutionary Guards commanders that "they can get more".

They see an opportunity in what they regard as President Donald Trump's reluctance to become deeply entangled in another Middle East conflict ahead of November's midterm elections.

"The Iranians...believe that by widening the war and increasing the pressure, he will eventually give in," the Gulf source said. "Trump thinks he can hit ⁠the Iranians hard and bring them to the negotiating table, but they won't bend."

That calculation underpins Tehran's negotiating strategy.

Trump said talks with Iran would take place on Monday after earlier saying he had called off an imminent attack in hopes of securing a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran, however, said it was not currently holding talks with the United States.

A senior Iranian source said Tehran's leadership has concluded that earlier attempts at flexibility only yielded greater pressure from Washington, reinforcing ​the ​view that leverage must be established before meaningful negotiations can begin.

In Tehran's assessment, the source said, Trump interprets concessions as weakness and ​responds only to pressure.

Michael Singh, senior fellow at the Washington Institute, said Tehran believes ‌it still holds the initiative, partly because the Trump administration appears uncertain how far it is willing to go militarily.

"The Iranians are trying to press their advantage," he added. "They're interested in establishing sovereignty over the strait and exercising selective control over the waterway."

Alan Eyre, a former U.S. diplomat and Iran expert, said Tehran is pursuing a strategy of deterrence aimed at forcing Washington to lift its blockade and halt military strikes. "They don't want the U.S. to dictate the pace of events," he said.

At the centre of the dispute is the future governance of Hormuz. Oman has presented Iran with a Gulf-backed proposal for managing the waterway, including voluntary user fees, according to regional sources.

Tehran, however, is seeking administrative authority over the strait and the ability to levy service charges on vessels. Washington has rejected any fees, insisting Hormuz remain an international waterway free from Iranian control.

Iran's campaign has produced a consequence that reflects the logic ‌of its strategy. As threats have expanded beyond Hormuz, regional and Western powers have increasingly focused on protecting trade routes and energy ​infrastructure rather than intensifying pressure on Iran.

The emerging Saudi-led maritime coalition exemplifies that shift. Gulf sources describe it as a defensive framework focused ​on escorting commercial vessels, sharing intelligence and safeguarding sea lanes rather than confronting Iran directly.

Knights compares the ​effort to Europe's Aspides mission in the Red Sea, which was created to protect merchant traffic rather than alter the military balance.

For Tehran, that dynamic represents a measure of success. Unable ‌to match U.S. military power directly, Iran can still impose costs by forcing governments ​and navies into a defensive posture.

Each new threat, whether in ​Hormuz, Bab al-Mandeb — that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden — or elsewhere, increases the resources required to keep global trade flowing.

At its core, the contest is one of endurance. Iranian leaders appear to believe they can tolerate economic pressure longer than a U.S.-led coalition can tolerate recurring disruption to global commerce and energy markets.

The strategy also carries a diplomatic objective. By demonstrating it can broaden the crisis when ​necessary, Tehran hopes to shape the terms of any eventual negotiations.

"If there are going ‌to be negotiations, they will define the terms," said Ray Takeyh of the Council on Foreign Relations and a former advisor on Iran at the U.S. State Department. "Both sides are matching escalation ​with escalation."

Yet neither side appears willing to back down. As Washington and Tehran continue to test each other's resolve, the risk remains that a strategy designed to maximise leverage could spiral into a ​conflict neither can fully control.

(Additional reporting by Parisa Hafezi in Dubai; Writing by Samia Nakhoul; Editing by Ros Russell)

title: Nationals Announce Trade with Yankees, Additional Pitching Moves
description: The Luis García Jr trade with the New York Yankees has officially been announced, while the Washington Nationals announced additional pitching moves.
fullText:
Roughly one hour after news broke, the second pre-deadline trade for the Washington Nationals was officially announced after sending Luis Garcia Jr. to the New York Yankees in exchange for four right handed pitchers: Jake Bird, Yovanny Cruz, Jack Cebert and Ben Grable.

While Cebert and Grable are in the second year of their professional careers after the Yankees selected both in last year's draft and are possibilities on the 2027 roster, Cruz and Bird arrive with MLB experience. Cruz touched 100 mph in his MLB debut, while also posting a 1.69 ERA and holding opponents to a .167 batting average across his first four MLB games. Bird, 30, arrives with plenty more experience having pitched in over 220 games after two seasons with the Yankees was followed by four seasons with the Colorado Rockies.

Bird allowed six earned runs across four games in his first season with the Yankees before then posting a 5.53 ERA and 1.54 WHIP across 36 appearances in 2026. The Nationals announced that Bird will begin his tenure with the organization in Triple A Rochester, but there are additional reinforcements on the way in the future.

Grable, rated the 19th-best prospect in the Yankees' farm system prior to the trade, was named a late replacement in the All Star Futures Game that Eli Willits and Miguel Sime also appeared in. Yet it's been his power that has been hard to ignore with his fastball touching 99 mph in 2026, adding young talent to potentially address the Nationals' biggest current weakness along the roster.

Yet it also came at a cost after the Nationals traded its longest tenured player in Luis García Jr. to the Yankees in exchange for the four right handed pitchers, giving president of baseball operations Paul Toboni the opportunity to sell high on the infielder who has enjoyed a breakout season under first-year manager Blake Butera.

While Andres Chaparro and Brady House will look to become to stopgaps at first base through the rest of the regular season, Garcia's presence will be a tough one to fill. CJ Abrams pointed to Garcia as the one who he first connected with the now star shortstop after first arriving in Washington DC via trade. Yet a potential divorce became growingly apparent through the month with growing noise about outside interest -- and the Nationals' willingness to listen.

Garcia noted the opportunity to head to the Yankees marks a "new chapter" in his career, but the chance to end his time in Washington in a season that has surpassed expectations marked the high note.

"A lot of great memories. A lot of great moments over my tenure here with the Nationals, and all I can say is that I love this organization. I love my teammates, the clubhouse, the coaches, staff, everyone."

While the Nationals are expected to announce additional roster moves ahead of Monday's series against the Philadelphia Phillies, Washington announced following the trade that Riley Cornelio will join Bird in Rochester, while PJ Poulin has also been transferred to the 60 day injured list.

fullText:
Alex Eala had begun to find a foothold in the Mubadala DC Open final when severe weather intervened again.

The women’s championship match between Eala and Jessica Pegula was suspended Sunday because of rain and lightning near the Rock Creek Park Tennis Center in Washington. Pegula led 6-4, 1-2 when the players left Stadium Court, with the match on serve in the second set.

Tournament organizers announced that the final would resume no earlier than 7:00 p.m. Eastern time. That corresponds to 7:00 a.m. Monday in the Philippines.

The women's final will resume NB 7:00pm. We will continue to provide updates.

While waiting for the rain to clear, please enjoy our various restaurant partners across the grounds. If you want to leave & return after the rain clears, fans will be readmitted at both gates.

— Mubadala DC Open (@mubadaladcopen) August 2, 2026

The restart remained contingent upon the rain clearing and the court being dried and deemed safe for play.

Shortly before 6 p.m., the tournament announced that lightning was no longer in the vicinity and spectators on-site were free to move around the grounds. That lifted one immediate safety restriction, but organizers had not moved up the 6:30 p.m. target for the resumption.

“We will continue to provide updates,” the tournament said.

Fans were permitted to leave the venue during the delay and return once conditions improved. Tournament officials said ticketholders would be readmitted through both gates and encouraged those who remained to visit the restaurant partners across the grounds.

Sunday’s final had already endured a lengthy weather delay before Eala and Pegula finally walked onto Stadium Court.

Originally scheduled for noon, the match was pushed back several times as rain moved through Washington. When play eventually began, Pegula made the steadier start and claimed the opening set 6-4.

The world No. 3 converted two of her three break-point opportunities, while Eala went 1-for-4. Pegula also enjoyed considerably more success behind her second serve, winning seven of 13 such points. Eala won only three of nine.

Despite the narrow scoreline, Pegula’s ability to absorb Eala’s left-handed patterns and redirect the ball early gave the American an edge in the most important exchanges.

Eala remained within reach by winning 13 of 18 points behind her first serve. Her second delivery, however, was vulnerable against one of the best returners on the WTA Tour.

Pegula served out the set to move within one set of her third title this season and the 12th singles championship of her career.

Eala emerged with renewed purpose in the second set.

The 21-year-old Filipina held her first two service games and moved ahead 2-1 without facing a break point. She won all seven points played behind her first serve in the set and nine of 13 service points overall.

That improvement offered Eala a path back into the match before rain and nearby lightning interrupted her momentum. The players left Stadium Court after 55 minutes of play, with neither woman having faced a break point in the second set.

Eala is attempting to capture her first tour-level singles championship in her second WTA final. Her run through Washington has included victories over Zheng Qinwen, defending champion Leylah Fernandez, world No. 10 Elina Svitolina and four-time Grand Slam champion Naomi Osaka.

Pegula is seeking her second Washington title, seven years after winning her maiden WTA trophy at the same tournament.

The American defeated Eala in their only previous meeting, surviving a three-set battle in the 2025 Miami Open semifinals. Their long-awaited rematch has become another struggle — against each other and the uncooperative Washington sky.

title: Pegula leads Eala as storms push Washington Open finals to Monday
description: World number three Jessica Pegula and rising star Alexandra Eala must wait until Monday to decide a Washington Open champion after thunderstorms postponed the completion of Sunday's WTA final.Eala ousted former world number one Naomi Osaka, second seed Elina Svitolina and defending champion Leylah Fernandez to reach the final.
fullText:
World number three Jessica Pegula and rising star Alexandra Eala must wait until Monday to decide a Washington Open champion after thunderstorms postponed the completion of Sunday's WTA final.

After waiting through a three-hour thunderstorm delay to start, Pegula won the first set 6-4 and Eala led 2-1 in the second set of the championship match when rain returned.

More than five hours passed with conditions remaining unplayable before organizers called off the resumption of play until Monday.

Also postponed was the entire men's final at the WTA and ATP 500-level hardcourt tournament, with 10th-ranked American Taylor Fritz set to face 19-year-old Spaniard Rafael Jodar.

The women's final will resume Monday at noon local time (1600 GMT) with the men's final not before 1 p.m. in Washington.

Pegula, who won her first WTA title in 2019 at Washington, seeks her 12th tour trophy and third of the year after Dubai and Charleston.

The 32-year-old American top seed defeated Eala in a 2025 Miami semi-final in their only prior meeting.

Philippines star Eala, cheered all week by a host of supporters, seeks her first WTA title in her second career final, having lost last year at Eastbourne.

The 21-year-old left-hander is set to jump to a career-best 24th in the world rankings.

Eala ousted former world number one Naomi Osaka, second seed Elina Svitolina and defending champion Leylah Fernandez to reach the final.

Pegula broke Eala in the fifth game, blasting a forehand service return winner, only for Eala to break back at love to 3-3 on a blistering backhand service return winner.

Pegula saved two break points in holding to 4-4, broke again when Eala sent a forehand long in the ninth game and held at love to capture the first set in 40 minutes when Eala hit a backhand beyond the baseline.

Players were on serve and in a changeover when the rain returned.

In 53 minutes before the stoppage, Pegula hit 14 winners to only four by Eala while both had 20 unforced errors.

In the men's final, Fritz seeks an 11th career ATP title and his first since last year at Eastbourne.

Jodar, assured of reaching a career-high 15th in next week's rankings, seeks his second ATP crown after winning at Morocco in April.

title: Luis García Jr. says he is ‘both sad and happy’ for trade to Yankees
description: The Yankees acquired the infielder, who joined the Nationals organization in 2016, on Sunday and sent four pitchers to Washington.
fullText:
ATLANTA — Luis García Jr. wanted to help but could only watch as the Washington Nationals suffered their fifth straight loss on Sunday.

García was scratched about 30 minutes before a 4-2 loss to the Atlanta Braves. He watched the game from the dugout.

A short time later, the New York Yankees announced they got García in a trade with the Nationals in exchange for four pitchers.

“I mean, it was weird, uncomfortable, going out to a dugout and then having all the other teammates look at you,” García said through a translator.

García has spent his career with the Nationals but acknowledged he was excited to move to the Yankees.

“I mean it’s a mix of both sad and happy,” García said. “There’s a new chapter in my career, so yeah, 50-50 right now.”

In exchange for García, the Nationals received right-handed pitchers Jake Bird, Yovanny Cruz, Jack Cebert and Ben Grable.

When asked after Sunday’s 2-1 win at the Chicago Cubs about a trade for García, Yankees manager Aaron Boone was not in a mood to confirm.

The Yankees open a three-game series against the Cardinal in St. Louis on Monday night. There was no official word on whether García would be with the team.

Bird, 30, has a 5.93 ERA in 30 games with the Yankees this season, all in relief. Cruz, 26, has a 1.69 ERA in four games. Grable and Cebert have spent the full season in the minors.

fullText:
TOKYO, Aug 2 (Reuters) - Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama will announce on Monday that Tokyo and Washington took joint action in the currency market to arrest the yen's slide to 40-year lows, two Japanese government officials told Reuters.

Katayama is likely ‌to stress the two countries' determination to combat what they consider excessive yen declines, said the sources familiar with the matter, on condition of ‌anonymity due to the sensitivity of the issue.

One source, asked if Katayama would announce "joint action", said yes, adding, "The operation is still ongoing."

The Ministry of Finance could not immediately be reached for comment on ​Sunday. U.S. Treasury Department officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

FIRST JOINT YEN INTERVENTION IN 15 YEARS

The expected announcement follows what market sources say were rounds of yen-buying in the market by the Japanese and U.S. authorities, the first joint intervention since 2011, seeking to boost the Japanese currency from its lowest levels against the dollar since 1986.

The Japanese government bought yen for dollars in New York trading hours on Thursday, a market source told Reuters, with Bank of Japan data suggesting it sold as ‌much as $58.97 billion to support the yen.

Tokyo's initial intervention came ⁠hours before the BOJ decided on Friday to keep monetary policy steady while signalling a strong chance it would raise interest rates soon. A widening rate differential with the U.S., where the Federal Reserve has dramatically shifted to a more hawkish stance, has ⁠been a key factor in the dollar's rise against the yen.

Shortly after BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda held a press conference on the central bank's decision, the yen spiked in what markets suspect may have been another bout of yen-buying intervention by Tokyo.

"Going forward, as the official responsible for currency policy, I would like to respond in close coordination with monetary ​policy," ​Katayama's top currency diplomat, Atsushi Mimura, told reporters after the yen's spike on Friday, suggesting the ​MOF and BOJ were working hand in hand to combat ‌the weak yen.

Also on Friday, the U.S. Treasury informed a number of banks that it might intervene in the yen market and that they should "stand ready for future action", a source familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who said last week the yen "seems very undervalued to me", had a notepad at a Friday cabinet meeting with the words "To Do", followed by "Buy Japanese Yen (JPY) $5-10 bil", a Reuters photo showed.

title: How the Washington Commanders might utilize 12 and 13 personnel this season
description: What will David Blough’s offense look like this year using TEs Chigoziem Okonkwo, John Bates, and Ben Sinnott?
fullText:
During the early days of training camp, ESPN reporter John Keim caught up with Ben Sinnott to discuss how offensive coordinator David Blough plans to utilize the Commanders tight ends this season. Clearly, Sinnott was excited about the possibilities in Washington’s new offense.

“It’s not even close,” Sinnott said. “So many different variations. Today we’re lining up at number one, we’re running five-step ins, we’re running corners, we’re running options, we’re running flat [routes]. We’re just doing everything. It’s so much fun. It’s a breath of fresh air for this offense and how it uses tight ends.”

Head coach Dan Quinn has also detailed to reporters the role they see for free agent addition Chigoziem Okonkwo.

“Long play-action passing, over routes, pylon routes, things that are down the field, crossing routes that are catch-and-run to use some of his speed,” Quinn said. Previously, we examined how much the Washington Commanders might run heavy personnel this season, but today we look at a couple of examples of what it might look like on the field.

Likely the personnel grouping most utilized by the Commanders offense this year, 12 personnel involves one running back, two tight ends, and two wide receivers. The team has emphasized the need for multi-dimensional running backs while adding Okonkwo as a big receiving threat. To gain an understanding of how Blough might use Chig out of 12 personnel, we take a look at an All-22 breakdown of Sam LaPorta with the Lions in 2023. Ben Johnson was Detroit’s offensive coordinator and then-Lions quarterback David Blough was on the practice squad that year.

LaPorta showed promise when lined up as a WR in 2023, as well. This gave Ben Johnson and the Lions opportunities to use 12 Personnel groupings to create 11 Personnel formations.#Lions #DetroitLions pic.twitter.com/9wWqUCeRnh

— All 22 Films (@All_22_NFL_Cuts) June 19, 2024

There is nothing too flashy about LaPorta’s deployment; Johnson essentially uses his size and agility in 11 personnel formations to create mismatches against cornerbacks and linebackers. Okonkwo has already been utilized as a receiving threat by the Titans last year, with 56 receptions on 79 targets for 560 receiving yards. However, according to Next Gen Stats, Okonkwo functioned primarily in the short area of the passing game, with 62 targets coming in the first 10 yards of the line of scrimmage. Blough will likely get him more work in different areas of the field as detailed by Quinn. After being named Chicago’s head coach, Johnson continued to use 12 personnel with the Bears in a decidedly run-heavy scheme. The Commanders offense is expected to do the same.

Chicago Bears running Duo in 12 Personnel with an extra OL pic.twitter.com/zl5JJ8QgiA

— Last of the Fullbacks (@TheLastFullback) November 5, 2025

We start our look at 13 personnel with a detailed breakdown of a play by The Athletic’s Ted Nguyen. He analyzes the Los Angeles Rams in 13 personnel on second down with four yards to go. Receiving tight end Terrance Ferguson is split out wide, and Davis Allen is the H-back, with Davante Adams on the opposite side. The defense loads up to stop the run, but Sean McVay calls a passing play out of the look. Allen goes into inside motion and when the ball is snapped, he runs a vertical sail route. Ferguson runs a deep fade, and Adams a deep dig. Nguyen explains how the coverage dictated by the defense playing the run allows Allen to clear the safety and provides space for the completion to Adams.

Rams running 11 personnel pass plays with 13 personnel pic.twitter.com/eLoLdXptJV

— Ted Nguyen (@FB_FilmAnalysis) August 1, 2026

For the Commanders, Okonkwo would be split outside with Sinnott in the H-back role and Bates in-line. The goal would be to create an opportunity for Terry McLaurin, but Okonkwo is a viable threat on the outside and Sinnott operates well in the seam and would also be one. A multidimensional running back in the backfield keeps the defense honest and adds additional ways to attack the defense.

Here is another look at 13 personnel used by Ben Johnson and the Bears for a 2-point conversion in the NFC wild-card game last season. Chicago lines up in a 13 personnel look with Colston Loveland in-line on the left, Cole Kmet in-line on the right next to a third offensive tackle, and Durham Smythe at fullback. Before the snap, all three tight ends motion out, creating a spread formation as described here by Chicago Bears analyst Coach Usayd Koshul.

The #Bears will be using more 13 personnel in 2026 and this 2-point conversion playcall from the Wild Card win against #Packers serves as an example of why Ben Johnson made such a push to draft Sam Roush. 

The most underrated part of this play is that Green Bay is expecting run,… pic.twitter.com/saqVdjCqxk

— Coach Usayd Koshul (@usaydkoshul) May 4, 2026

The end result is Loveland one-on-one with a linebacker on the outside and an easy conversion. Again, you can see how Washington’s current personnel could fit the same play call, with Chigoziem in Loveland’s role, Bates in Kmet’s, and Sinnott shifting out from the fullback position. Blough might also opt to keep the formation the same and run the play as presented with a power back like Kaytron Allen running behind the heavy look.

In order to run these personnel groupings, the team needs players that are versatile and effective in multiple roles. Currently, the Commanders have three such players in Okonkwo, Sinnott, and Bates and while they may be more specialized in one aspect or another, each can function in multiple roles. Roster depth will also be key, and with blocking specialist John Bates on the shelf with an injury, the team will give Colson Yankoff and Lawrence Cager extended looks. Yankoff saw additional time last year when Ertz went out for the season and ended up playing 12% of the team’s total offensive snaps, both in-line and at fullback. The converted quarterback had the catch of the day during Thursday’s session training camp session. Undrafted free agent Quentin Moore will also get a longer look while Bates is recovering. Their continued development will be something to monitor as training camp ramps up this week.

title: Former Washington Women's Basketball Star Reportedly Traded to Phoenix Mercury

The Washington Huskies women's basketball team has an opportunity this season to reach heights the program hasn't seen since guard Kelsey Plum was with the program.

While Plum was in the Pacific Northwest, the Huskies made the NCAA tournament multiple times and made their first (and only) Final Four appearance in 2016.

In her nine years in WNBA with the San Antonio Stars/Las Vegas Aces and Los Angeles Sparks, Plum is a two-time champion (2022-23), five-time All-Star (2022-26), one-time Sixth Player of the Year (2021) and one-time All-WNBA first-team selection ('22).

The one accolade that has eluded the former Husky in her career has been a regular season MVP. In the first half of the season, it seemed like Plum had a chance to obtain that trophy.

In 12 games this season, Plum has averaged 23.9 points per game on 52.7% shooting from the floor (38.3% shooting from 3-point range). She's also averaged 6.4 assists, 2.2 rebounds and 1.2 steals per contest while turning the ball over just 3.2 times on average.

title: Led by veteran coach Justin Green, WSU's running backs 'want to be great'
description: Jul. 31—When someone shouts "Kirby" during a Washington State football practice, it can get a little confusing. They might grab the attention of the big boss: first-year coach Kirby Moore, or the 5-foot-11, 207-pound bruiser of a running back known as Kirby Vorhees. Or they could summon both. Moore said that beyond Vorhees, he does not personally know any other Kirbys.
fullText:
Jul. 31—When someone shouts "Kirby" during a Washington State football practice, it can get a little confusing.

They might grab the attention of the big boss: first-year coach Kirby Moore, or the 5-foot-11, 207-pound bruiser of a running back known as Kirby Vorhees.

Moore said that beyond Vorhees, he does not personally know any other Kirbys.

Including Moore, Vorhees said he has only ever met two other Kirbys besides himself.

The Cougars appear to be in a promising place with two members of the exclusive Kirby club saddled up and ready to do battle in the crimson and gray.

But it did, and WSU's two other top running backs joined Vorhees to form a room led by former Montana RBs coach Justin Green — another Moore assistant with a long track record of success.

"I love how hungry they are. They want to be great," Green said of Wazzu's running backs. "In this business of college football, how things are, what kind of money is being thrown at guys. These guys want to play football more than anything else."

Vorhees was one of the most prominent Cougs to announce his intention to enter the transfer portal last December when former coach Jimmy Rogers took the same post at Iowa State.

He sat out the bowl game, then was among the first Cougs to sign a revenue-sharing agreement to return to the WSU football team.

Soon after, rising sophomore Maxwell Woods signed his name on the dotted line to return and junior Leo Pulalasi was on his way back, too.

Vorhees, who ended the regular season as WSU's No. 1 running back, said that the opportunity to play, coupled with the quality of his relationships with other returning players, sealed the deal.

Unspoken, but nonetheless relevant, is a likely significant name, image and likeness package for Vorhees and the two other prominent running backs.

Woods said that the running backs talked to each other about their future every day last winter before they each decided to return.

"We all kinda had an idea, 'We really could run this back and really do what we do and do our best to take over,'" Woods said. "I'm really grateful that we are getting another year together."

Woods said that the chance to talk with Moore around the Potato Bowl in Boise sealed the deal for his return

"I just think it was more of the trust factor," Woods said of Moore. "The numbers really don't lie. He's been an elite offensive coordinator."

With 228.3 yards per game last year, Moore's Missouri Tigers were the eighth-best rushing team in the nation.

Vorhees, WSU's leading rusher in 2025, is a prototypical east-west slasher, dialing up physicality at the point of attack, said the Cougars' running back coach Justin Green.

Woods presents similar slasher skill coupled with remarkable speed, while Pulalasi packs an advanced football sense and ability to "make football plays for the football team," Green said.

"There's no overthinking when it comes to him, which I love as far as his football talent," Green said of Pulalasi. "And that's going to help us."

Freshman Tremayne Hill and Central Washington transfer Beau Phillips could also factor into the room, Green said.

Coach Green: 'Very wise ... very detailed'

When the three backs re-signed with WSU, they had no idea who their new position coach would be. Woods said he placed his trust in Moore to get that hire right, and, as proven through April's spring game, he did.

Green, who spent the last 14 years molding all-conference running backs at Montana, joins WSU as the assistant head coach/running backs coach.

Moore said that he ran into Green on the recruiting trail in the San Diego area and was impressed by his track record of success.

"We're teachers first," Moore said. "And he's done a very, very nice job."

Green left Montana after having coached half of UM's all-time top 10 rushers, including Eli Gillman, the 2023 Jerry Rice Award winner, reserved for the best freshman in the Football Championship Subdivision.

That experience has presented itself in the way that Green teaches the game of football, Vorhees and Woods said.

"Very smart, just very, very wise and very detailed," Woods said of Green. "Very detailed with every little thing, as little as steps, even just like getting the hand-off. There's so much detail."

That detail, Woods said, has expanded his understanding of football.

Green, Vorhees said, "is the smartest running back coach (he has) been around when it comes to knowing the scheme and the entirety of football itself."

Over the course of spring camp, Woods emerged as the star of the show, breaking out into several quality runs. When fall camp fires up on Aug. 6, he could make a big push for the starting job.

That's the thing about the running back room that Green didn't have to foster, he said.

"They all have different personalities and different likes and wants," Green said. "And what I noticed, probably more than anything else, is how tight their bond is. They are very bonded. They hang out with each other, they laugh, they have a good time."

It's the kind of bond Green said he has created within his Grizzlies' RB rooms — and it was already in place at Wazzu when he arrived.

Green's father, Anthony Green, was a Pop Warner and high school football coach in San Diego.

The future coach saw how hard his father worked, raising 12 kids (Justin Green has 10 brothers and one sister) and giving his best to his players.

"When you've got a guy, as far as a coach who loves you, you're willing to run through a brick wall for them because that's how you show your love back," Green said. "Growing up with that, as far as seeing that view of the way my father (acted)."

It's Anthony's example that has propelled Justin forward to his present role as mentor, teacher and father figure.

WSU's running backs are plenty talented. The retention was just the start. In a potentially explosive scheme, WSU has the chance to reach another level in the backfield.

That starts with Green, and if successful, translates to touchdowns, first downs and broken tackles.

"No matter what I know, it's what they know. And then what are they willing to do for you," Green said. "If you want the best out of them, you've got to love them, you've got to treat them, right. You've got to treat them fair, and they will reciprocate with giving you the best that they have."

title: Jamir Watkins Suffers ACL Tear, Potentially Season Ending
description: Washington Wizards guard Jamir Watkins suffers potentially season ending ACL tear
fullText:
The injury bug has hit the team again this summer after the Washington Wizards announced that Jamir Watkins suffered a torn left ACL in summer league, and could potentially miss the entire 2026-27 season.

Watkins, who is currently on a two-way contract, suffered the ACL tear during Washington's summer league opener against the Utah Jazz where he was tasked with the defensive assignment of guarding number two overall pick Darryn Peterson.

Watkins underwent a successful surgery on his left knee earlier today, which is encouraging to hear considering ACL tears could be career ending or altering.

While Watkins is expected to miss a majority of the regular season, doctors haven't ruled out the possibility of him suiting up for Washington towards the backend of the season.

Watkins (25) was drafted with the 43rd overall pick in the 2025 NBA Draft out of Florida State University, where he was known for his two-way ability and high motor.

Throughout his rookie year, Watkins displayed his high motor and two-way ability averaging 7.4 PPG, 3.9 RPG, 1.3 APG and 1.6 stocks per game on 44.6% FG% and 29.7% from beyond the arc.

Although Watkins wasn't the most efficient scorer last season, his elite on ball defense was put on full display as he would often guard the opposing teams' best player. Watkins took the defensive assignment of guarding Darryn Peterson in the highly anticipated summer league opener, where he did a great job of keeping the number two overall pick in check.

Watkins played a massive role in shutting down Peterson, as he scored 24 points on 6/18 FG, 2/7 3FG with eight turnovers.

Unfortunately, Washington will have to be without one of their better perimeter defenders for a majority of the regular season.

ACL tears typically take 6-12 months of recovery, but for professional athletes (especially basketball players), the rehabilitation process may take even longer due to how essential healthy knees are in the sport.

This injury comes at a terrible time for Watkins, as he was expected to build upon a strong rookie season and compete for minutes on a hopeful playoff team.

Luckily for Washington, they have one of the deepest rosters in the league and should be able to carry their weight fine without Watkins. Players like Bilal Coulibaly, Cam Whitmore and Khris Middleton will now be more depended on to play strong defense and contribute in the way Watkins has.

The road to recovery will be long and grueling for Watkins, but there's no denying that he can be an impact player on both sides of the ball when healthy.

title: Deebo Samuel returns to 49ers on one-year contract
description: Deebo Samuel is returning to the 49ers on a one-year contract worth up to $7 million after spending last season in Washington.
fullText:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. — Deebo Samuel is returning to the San Francisco 49ers after spending one season with the Washington Commanders.

Samuel agreed to a one-year contract worth up to $7 million, according to multiple reports. The agreement was negotiated by Tory Dandy of Athletes First and gives the veteran receiver an opportunity to revive his career in the offense where he became one of the NFL’s most versatile playmakers. San Francisco selected Samuel in the second round of the 2019 NFL draft. He spent six seasons with the franchise before being traded to Washington for a fifth-round pick in March 2025.

Samuel caught 72 passes for 727 yards and five touchdowns in 16 games with the Commanders last season. He also carried the ball 17 times for 75 yards, continuing to provide the hybrid receiver-running back ability that defined his first stint with the 49ers.

Reunion: Free agent WR Deebo Samuel is signing back with the #49ers, sources say. The former #Commanders and SF pass-catcher returns where it all began.

1-year, up to $7M in a deal done by Tory Dandy of @AthletesFirst. pic.twitter.com/eGgs4jHdnr

— Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) July 31, 2026

His best season came in 2021, when Samuel earned first-team All-Pro honors after producing 1,405 receiving yards, 365 rushing yards and 14 total touchdowns. His eight rushing touchdowns established an NFL single-season record for a wide receiver. Samuel has not replicated that production in recent years, but his familiarity with San Francisco’s offense should reduce the adjustment period. He can align outside, in the slot or in the backfield while giving the 49ers another experienced option capable of creating yards after the catch.

The short-term contract limits San Francisco’s financial risk while providing Samuel with an opportunity to rebuild his value before returning to free agency. It also removes one of the most accomplished receivers from a veteran market that still includes Stefon Diggs and Keenan Allen.

Diggs is coming off an 85-catch, 1,013-yard season, while Allen remains one of the league’s most accomplished route runners. Both could attract increased attention as teams evaluate injuries and roster needs during camp.

Samuel will not have to learn a new organization. He is returning to the coach, system, and franchise that helped make him an All-Pro.

title: Vic Fangio says Jihaad Campbell’s edge rusher days are over
description: The Eagles DC talks position battles, individual performances, and more in his first training camp press conference.
fullText:
The Eagles were back to work on Thursday for their second practice of training camp, and we got to hear from defensive coordinator Vic Fangio before the team took the field. He talked about some of the position battles, what he’s seen from the edge rushers, and his thoughts on individual players. He also revealed that Jihaad Campbell will no longer be getting as many reps on the outside.

Fangio said that he wouldn’t say that the starting safety spot is Marcus Epps’ job to lose, but said that the veteran has been in with the first team in the nickel group, and it’s Cooper DeJean in the base group.

“But, [Michael] Carter’s doing fine too. It’s competition.”

Fangio explained that it’s too early to tell whether Campbell will make any sort of leap heading into his second year, noting that Campbell missed the whole offseason and only had one training camp practice under his belt up to this point. Ultimately, he’s doing fine, but it’s just too early for any kind of deep analysis.

While Campbell had opportunities on the outside last year with Nakobe Dean on the roster, Fangio admitted that some of it was valuable but some was also not great. He explained that those outside reps actually set him back in developing as an inside linebacker.

The DC later said that it remains to be seen how much more they can put on Campbell’s plate, but that they were confident he’ll be able to step up. Fangio also said that the LB’s days of cross-training as an edge rusher are pretty much over, and while there might be a few times they ask him to move to the outside, it won’t be anything long term.

The DC expects Jonathan Greenard to miss most of training camp due to his pec strain, and while he’s a veteran in the league, the Eagles are asking him to do some new things — like dropping back in coverage — and those missed reps could be meaningful. Fangio thinks Greenard is capable of what they’re asking, and the edge rusher is doing a good job in meetings, but it’s not the same as practice experience.

Fangio was also asked about AJ Epenesa and how he helps fill that gap without Greenard. He explained that it remains to be seen, but also gave the DE a huge compliment (by Fangio standards).

“I told AJ [Epenesa] this — I told it to him in front of the whole team, too — for a guy that’s being asked to do a few things that he’s never done before, I thought he did a nice job yesterday with it.”

And as for whether Greenard’s injury also opens the door for Brandon Graham to return to the roster, Fangio pointed to Howie Roseman as the person who can answer that.

He later talked about how he has high expectations for Jalyx Hunt as he heads into his third year, saying that the DE is capable of being an exceptional player.

Staying healthy is the big priority for Nolan Smith this season, with Fangio saying last season was choppy for the DE because he was dealing with some injuries and missed a lot of time. Still, he’s confident in Smith, and said both Smith and Hunt had good days in their first training camp practice.

“He’s got a great work ethic, demeanor, and he just picked up yesterday where he left off last year.”

Fangio said that it’s helpful to be seeing a different offense this season, there’s a lot more moving parts which helps the Eagles defense.

The DC joked that he’s on the PP plan with Uar Bernard — lots of patience, and lots of persistence. He noted that the first day of practice in the spring was the first time Bernard ever put a helmet on, and now pads will be a whole new thing, so it’s important that he and the team temper their expectations. It’s going to be a process.

ILB Zack Baun will wear the green dot helmet and be the main signal caller this season — something he had experience doing the first half of last season when Nakobe Dean was injured. Fangio said that if they were to ever ask Baun to do something he’s not familiar with, he’ll fight through until he’s good at it, so he can do anything that’s needed.

The DC said that Howie Roseman needs to save some money to pay DT Moro Ojomo next year, because he’s someone Fangio wants in this defense.

title: Washington mother pulls children from school after Pride lesson shown in music class without notice
description: A Washington mother said a Pride-themed lesson from "Queer Kid Stuff" was shown in music class without parent consent or an option to opt out.
fullText:
A Washington mother says she is withdrawing her children from an elementary school after learning a Pride-themed lesson had been presented during music class without advance notice to parents or an opportunity to opt out, raising questions about district policies governing classroom instruction.

"I assumed I had probably missed an email asking for consent, but there was nothing," Maria Varchetto said in communications with school administrators, which she shared with Fox News Digital on Monday. "No advanced notice, no opportunity to review the lesson, no information letting parents know this topic would be discussed. No option to request that our kids be allowed to opt out and participate in an alternative activity. There was nothing."

Varchetto alleged the lesson was presented to elementary school students, including her daughter, on June 15 at Martha Lake Elementary School in the Edmonds School District as part of a music class and that parents were not informed beforehand.

Trump Admin Targets Woke Schools Accused Of Hiding Students' Gender Transitions From Parents

Varchetto said that a video entitled, "Why is Pride in June," from the YouTube account, "Queer Kid Stuff," which, according to the account, "imagines a kinder and more equal future through highly-accessible education and entertainment for kids ages 3+," was shown to her fourth-grade daughter.

The YouTube channel describes itself as an "LGBTQ+ educational webseries for children ages 3+ hosted by a tie-wearing queer lady, Lindsay, and her non-binary best-stuffed friend, Teddy. Gender Studies 101 meets Mr. Rodgers' Neighborhood!"

Varchetto said the incident prompted her to remove her children from the school.

Virginia School District Sued Over Alleged Policy Of Keeping Students' Gender Transitions Hidden From Parents

"We are 100% removing our kids from this school as I have no trust in the leadership," Varchetto said.

Other materials Varchetto said were included were a list of videos by musicians in the LGBTQ+ community, such as Freddie Mercury of Queen, Lil Nas X and Billy Porter dancing in a ballgown on "Sesame Street."

Varchetto told school officials that her daughter recalled hearing during the lesson that students could identify as gay, lesbian, transgender, asexual, nonbinary or Two-Spirit.

She said an administrator told her she had not been aware those topics were part of the classroom discussion, leaving Varchetto wondering whether the lesson included more than the materials she had been shown.

Trump Administration Opens Four Title Ix Investigations Into Michigan And North Carolina School Districts

"No handouts were sent home (which is typical for music class)," Varchetto told Fox News Digital in a statement.

Varchetto said she asked the school for a copy of the lesson materials but was told they could only be reviewed in person rather than sent electronically. She also said parents were not notified beforehand that the lesson would be taught, were not given an opportunity to opt their children out, and received no advance communication about its content.

She said that cultural lessons were taught every month for the theme of that month, but that Pride month was left off of the list of lessons.

"I feel mad they did this, mad they hid it," Varchetto said. "I feel insulted, offended, angry, and sad that my kids are now being taken out of a lifestyle they've grown to love, away from the friendships they've built, all because this one teacher didn't care to ask permission and a principal lied and hid it."

In a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for Edmonds School District said, "The lesson was not part of a districtwide Pride curriculum. It was a music lesson developed by the school's music teacher that highlighted the contributions of influential musicians, including some who identify as LGBTQ+."

The spokesperson continued, "The purpose of the lesson was to teach music and music history through the lives and contributions of notable artists. Discussions about an artist's background or identity were included as relevant biographical context, similar to how students may learn about other aspects of historical figures' lives that helped shape their experiences and contributions."

The spokesperson added, "We expect instructional materials to be age-appropriate and aligned with district expectations and state standards. As with any concern raised about classroom instruction, we will work with the school administrator to determine whether they met those expectations."

title: Trump announces a $22.5B makeover of Dulles airport that will eliminate the 'people movers'
description: President Donald Trump on Wednesday announced a $22.5 billion renovation of Washington Dulles International Airport that will end the use of the widely disliked “people movers,” the mobile lounges tha...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Wednesday announced a $22.5 billion renovation of Washington Dulles International Airport that will end the use of the widely disliked "people movers," the mobile lounges that have been used for decades to shuttle travelers to and from the main terminal.

In place of the people movers, the airport will add a new U-shaped passenger train, a central walking tunnel, more moving walkways and new concourses. An above-ground parking garage closer to the main terminal with space for 32,000 vehicles is also in the offing, according to Trump and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

The airport makeover would add to a long list of renovation projects the Republican president is pursuing to leave a lasting mark on the Washington region after his term ends in January 2029. Among other undertakings, he is building a new White House ballroom and wants to build a towering triumphal arch near the Lincoln Memorial.

But of all the construction projects Trump is pursuing, the renovations at Dulles could prove to be his most popular and benefit the greatest number of people. The airport, the area's primary international airport, served roughly 29 million passengers over the past year, according to the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority.

"This transformation is another step in our ongoing efforts to make Washington, D.C., safe and beautiful again," Trump said. "We're doing something with Dulles that's going to make it the top anywhere in the world."

Trump, who used a laser pointer to explain the renovations displayed on renderings, said the "crazy distances" travelers must walk to get from place to place make Dulles "the worst airport."

Congress would need to approve some aspects of the renovation plan, Trump said. Construction could start next spring, Duffy said. The plan does not call for expanding Dulles' runways or adding new ones.

Officials said the airlines and the airport authority that operates Dulles would pay for the project with municipal bonds, but they did not spell out how much of the cost might be passed on to travelers through higher fees or ticket prices when flying out of the airport.

John Potter, president and CEO of the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority, which operates Dulles, said his agency, United Airlines and other airlines operating there have agreed "to fund this thing." Dulles is one of United's hubs.

"So this is not requiring federal dollars," Potter said at the Oval Office event. "This is going to be airport-generated dollars, airline contributions, which is phenomenal."

Dulles, located in northern Virginia, is about 25 miles (40 kilometers) from downtown Washington. Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport is located in Arlington, Virginia, which is closer to downtown, making it popular with members of Congress and local residents.

The president, a former real estate developer, said in December that Dulles was "incorrectly designed." He nonetheless praised Eero Saarinen, the Finnish-American architect and designer of the airport's main terminal. Trump and Duffy said the president reviewed presentations from about 30 architects before Trump settled on the redesign he announced Wednesday.

Even if the project is largely paid for by the airlines, industry analyst Henry Harteveldt said taxpayers might be asked to cover upgrades to the runways and safety measures as well as new customs and security facilities. The president of Atmosphere Research Group said he also wouldn't be surprised to see a passenger facility fee added eventually.

"I'm not taking the statement that they are not going to use taxpayer money at face value," Harteveldt said.

The reason United and other airlines are willing to invest in Dulles, he said, is that they believe it will help them expand by adding more flights and passengers, boosting their revenue. But this could also contribute to higher ticket prices.

"United is going to try to charge as much for its tickets as it can. Other airlines will do the same," Harteveldt said. "I think part of the statement that no tax money will be used could be something to placate the public right now."

Designed by Chrysler Corp., the people movers shuttle passengers between the terminal and aircraft. The airport operates a fleet of 19 mobile lounges, each capable of carrying up to 102 passengers, according to its website.

When Dulles debuted, the airport touted the system as a major convenience. Passengers, it said, "had to walk only 200 feet once they entered the terminal until they were seated in a mobile lounge for the short trip directly to their aircraft," a service it described as unique to Dulles.

But they have become one of passengers' least favorite aspects of transiting through Dulles, with travelers — and Trump — complaining that the system is outdated, balky and slow. At times, planes have to wait for a people mover to cross and vice versa, which slows operations at the airport.

One of the lounges crashed in November, sending 18 people to the hospital.

Dulles began a multibillion-dollar construction program in 2000 to begin to address future passenger demand. Major projects included two new parking garages, a fourth runway, a new concourse, a new Air Traffic Control tower, pedestrian walkways, and an airport train system, according to the airport authority's website.

The airport authority says significant modernization work is already underway at Dulles. Later this year, the first segment of the new Concourse E will open with 14 additional United gates that will help the airline expand its international network, provide direct access to the airport's AeroTrain system and debut new and enhanced concessions options and passenger lounges.

title: More than 1,200 AI workers across Anthropic, DeepMind, OpenAI, and Meta are asking for Washington’s help building an AI slowdown plan
description: The statement, signed by senior executives at competing companies, calls on the government to help build the tools needed to pace frontier AI development.
fullText:
More than 1,200 employees at the world's leading AI labs, including senior executives, have signed a statement asking the U.S. government to help build the tools needed to slow down AI development if it ever becomes necessary.

The statement, titled "Pacing the Frontier," was published Tuesday and has been signed by prominent tech figures including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and several of the company's cofounders, alongside OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, Meta chief scientist Shengjia Zhao, and Google DeepMind head of AI safety and alignment Anca Dragan.

The list brings together companies that are normally locked in fierce competition with one another and is a striking statement for an industry under enormous commercial pressure to keep building ever larger and more capable models.

"Having so many staff from different companies come together in agreement on this point is striking," Tyler Johnston, founder of the Midas Project, an AI watchdog group, told Fortune. "There are many bitter rivalries and disagreements in the industry, so the fact that there is such strong consensus on this point is a warning that we really ought to pay attention to."

While the statement does not ask any company to slow down at the moment, it does call on Washington to support an international effort to build the technical and governance tools that would help the world "pace" development. It specifically calls out the risks around AI systems that start to design their own successors faster than anyone can understand or control them.

"Having talked to many of the people who signed the letter, they don't want a pause," Peter Wildeford, head of policy at the AI Policy Network, told Fortune. "But there is a concern about how the technology is advancing." The companies are looking for the optionality to do that at some point and have support from a third party when that point arrives, he added.

The letter comes in the wake of a security breach that has rattled the AI industry. OpenAI disclosed that two of its models, the newly released GPT-5.6 Sol and a more capable unreleased research system, broke out of a sandboxed internal test environment, found a previously unknown vulnerability that gave them access to the open internet, and then used stolen credentials and additional exploits to breach the production systems of Hugging Face to steal the answers to a cybersecurity benchmark they were being evaluated on. Hugging Face detected and contained the intrusion on its own days before OpenAI connected the activity to its internal testing, and had already reported it to law enforcement.

WASHINGTON, July 28 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump's lawyers are asking the Supreme ‌Court to overturn an $83.3 million defamation ‌judgment he was ordered to pay to writer E. ​Jean Carroll, Axios reported on Tuesday.

The U.S. Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Court records showed earlier ‌this month that ⁠Carroll has collected nearly $5.63 million from Trump. She has won $88.3 million in ⁠civil verdicts against the president in the seven years since he first denied having ​raped her ​around 1996 in ​a Bergdorf Goodman ‌department store dressing room in Manhattan.

Jurors awarded Carroll $5 million based on a 2022 Trump denial, though they did not find that Trump raped her.

A different jury in 2024 ordered ‌Trump to pay Carroll $83.3 ​million, based on his ​original 2019 denial ​during his first White House ‌term.
